message:
Nice catch, Derek. I have the fourth edition, and am familiar with the second edition, and didn't bother to check Lyons's reference. Apparently, neither did he. This -- as my description of the panel may have suggested -- seems generally characteristic of the three presentations: the presenters had a theoretical agenda and simply ignored whatever didn't fit. It might have taken Lyons an afternoon to trace the comings and goings of authors in various editions of *WoR*; the failure to do so seems to me emblematic of a general critical carelessness on the part of the panel.

Now, my gut feeling is that Lyons *was* right in his thesis that composition as a field has found the problems of alienation too thorny to adequately address, and so has shifted its attention to the more friendly concerns of hybridity, multiculturalism, and border-crossing globalization. (In fact, this is sort of what I said a while ago in [my](/weblog/2003/08/12/seitz-class-analysis-part-1.html) [critique](/weblog/2003/08/13/seitz-class-analysis-part-2.html) of Seitz's construction of critical pedagogy.) The problem is, he -- like his peers on the panel -- let Hardt and Negri do the theoretical work without any careful and sustained attempts to struggle with how such theories might intersect with concrete pedagogical practice.

If nothing else, it stands as a useful cautionary example.
